1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 exd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6.name: Scotch Game: Schmidt Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 exd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6.background: 4...Nf6 was first recorded in an article by Eugen von Schmidt in the January 1865 issue of the Schachzeitung, and the variation carries his name.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 exd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6.strategy: Develops with a threat to e4, so White must decide how to meet it. The usual answer trades knights and leaves Black with doubled c-pawns, a structural flaw balanced by free development and the half-open b-file.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 exd4 4.Nxd4 Bc5.name: Scotch Game: Classical Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 exd4 4.Nxd4 Bc5.strategy: Puts the question to the d4 knight at once: it must be traded, defended or moved. Black develops with tempo and sets the pace, aiming for easy equality, but White chooses how to answer.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 exd4 4.Nxd4 Qh4.name: Scotch Game: Steinitz Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 exd4 4.Nxd4 Qh4.background: Wilhelm Steinitz popularised 4...Qh4, and the variation carries his name.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 exd4 4.Nxd4 Qh4.strategy: Hits e4 and f2 at once and can win a pawn, but the queen comes out early and White gains time developing against it. Black's king risks being stuck in the centre, and White's lead in development more than pays for the pawn.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 exd4 4.Nxd4 Bb4+.name: Scotch Game: Malaniuk Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 exd4 4.Nxd4 Bb4+.strategy: Checks to provoke a concession: the natural reply c3 gains White a tempo but takes the best square from the b1 knight. Black steps out of main-line theory in return for the lost time, a playable surprise that sidesteps well-trodden paths.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 exd4 4.Nxd4 Nxd4.strategy: Trades knights, but White recaptures with the queen, which settles on a central square where Black cannot easily chase it. Sound enough, yet Black spends time to give White the more active development and the easier game.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 exd4 4.Nxd4 Bc5 5.strategy: Guards the d4 knight with a developing move and keeps the strongpoint in the centre. It carries a small trap: 5...Nf6? loses a piece to Nxc6 followed by Bxc5. White holds a solid grip on the centre and Black has to find the right plan.

Trades the attacked knight at once, with tempo because the knight on c6 also attacks the queen. White simplifies and removes the pressure on d4. The cost is that Black's in-between move ...Qf6 threatens mate on f2 immediately.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 exd4 4.Nxd4 Bc5 5.name: Scotch Game: Potter Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 exd4 4.Nxd4 Bc5 5.background: The line is named after William Norwood Potter. It was revived in the 2000s with success by Vassily Ivanchuk and Magnus Carlsen.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 exd4 4.Nxd4 Bc5 5.strategy: Saves the knight and attacks the bishop in one move, so Black has to spend time with it. The knight is passive on b3 but safe, and White develops calmly, often castling long, instead of entering the early skirmishes of the lines with Be3.

Adds a third attacker to the d4 knight, which White must now defend a third time. The queen comes out early but with tempo, and all of Black's pieces point at the centre. White's usual reply holds everything together.

Sidesteps the exchange by retreating the bishop, a choice for players who have seen the tactic against the natural developing move. It gives up the pressure on the d4 knight, so White can swing the knight to attack g7 and keeps a comfortable game.
Natural development, but it loses a piece: 6.Nxc6 attacks the queen and uncovers the e3-bishop against the bishop on c5. After 6...dxc6 7.Qxd8+ Kxd8 8.Bxc5 White has won a piece.

Defends the d4 knight a third time with a pawn, which neutralises Black's pressure and lets White build a broad pawn centre. The cost is a slightly passive queen's knight, which loses its natural square.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 exd4 4.Nxd4 Bc5 5.name: Scotch Game: Blumenfeld Attack
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 exd4 4.Nxd4 Bc5 5.strategy: Threatens Nxc7+, forking king and rook, and leads to a wild trade: after ...Bxe3 fxe3 Qh4+ g3 Qxe4 each side wins a rook in the corner. The result is balanced, but it is far riskier than the solid c3.

Defends d4 a second time, but d4 is attacked three times, by the knight, the bishop and the queen, and defended only twice. After 6...Nxd4 7.Bxd4 Bxd4 White cannot recapture without losing the queen, and is a piece down.

The main line: the knight develops where it guards c6, and the queen keeps its grip on d4 and f2 while Black prepares to castle. Black accepts a solid but slightly cramped position, since White has more space.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 exd4 4.Nxd4 Bc5 5.name: Scotch Game: Classical Variation, Millennium Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 exd4 4.Nxd4 Bc5 5.strategy: Sidesteps the main line: the queen swings to g6 to attack e4 at once, and the g8 knight stays free to come out to f6. The cost is that the queen no longer adds pressure on d4 and f2, so White has time to organise.

A solid pawn move that frees the c8-bishop, but it cuts the queen's protection of the knight on c6, so White can trade there at once. Black then either accepts damaged pawns on the c-file or exchanges bishops on e3 first, which wrecks White's pawns as well: playable but less harmonious than the main line.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 exd4 4.Nxd4 Bc5 5.name: Scotch Game: Romanishin Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 exd4 4.Nxd4 Bc5 5.strategy: Develops with check instead of retreating the bishop to b6, forcing White to block. After the usual c3 the bishop retreats to e7, a safe but unambitious route that steps away from the main Potter lines.

The natural retreat: the bishop stays on the diagonal aimed at f2 and out of reach of b4 and d4, while White's knight has been pushed back to b3. Black gets a healthy, flexible position and loses nothing in development.

Offers a trade instead of retreating, but after Nxc5 Qxc5 Black has given up the bishop pair for nothing. White then gains space with c4 and keeps both bishops, which leaves Black passive against a clear edge.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 exd4 4.Nxd4 Bc5 5.name: Scotch Game: Classical Variation, Intermezzo Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 exd4 4.Nxd4 Bc5 5.strategy: An in-between move: the queen threatens mate on f2, so White must deal with that first and cannot save the knight on c6. Black then retakes at leisure, usually with the d-pawn, which avoids an isolated a-pawn.
A natural recapture towards the centre: Black gets doubled c-pawns, but an open b-file and active pieces. It leads to a solid, roughly level game and avoids the sharper in-between move.
Recaptures with the d-pawn, but lets White swap queens at once with Qxd8+, and after Kxd8 Black has lost the right to castle for no compensation. The king stays stuck in the centre.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 exd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5.strategy: Trades the knight and aims to leave Black with doubled c-pawns, since retaking with the d-pawn lets White trade queens and strip Black of castling. White gets a lasting structural plus but must look after the e4 pawn, which the f6 knight attacks.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 exd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5.name: Scotch Game: Alekhine Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 exd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5.strategy: Pushes at the f6 knight and offers the pawn: after ...Nxe5 White's queen and bishop come out with tempo against the e5 knight. The game stays level, so it is sound, but it costs a pawn to reach what the quiet Nxc6 or Nc3 keep.

Defends e4 with a developing move instead of trading on c6, so the knights stay on and the game turns calm and balanced. White can still saddle Black with doubled c-pawns later, while Black develops without trouble.
The only good recapture: ...dxc6 allows a queen trade that costs Black the right to castle. Black accepts doubled c-pawns for the half-open b-file and a pawn on c6 that watches the b5 and d5 squares.
Recaptures with the d-pawn and opens the d-file, which lets White trade queens with check. Black has to recapture with the king and loses the right to castle, while the doubled c-pawns stay.
Grabs the e4 pawn but ignores the knight on c6, which takes the queen on d8. Black can only recapture the knight, so the queen is lost for a pawn.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 exd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5.name: Scotch Game: Mieses Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 exd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5.background: Jacques Mieses played the line repeatedly at Hastings 1895, including a first-round win over Joseph Henry Blackburne, and those games contributed to the variation being named after him. Garry Kasparov has played it frequently.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 exd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5.strategy: Drives the knight away with tempo and grabs space, at the price of an advanced pawn that Black's queen can attack at once. Sharp, forcing play follows: White has the space, Black has a target in the e5 pawn.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 exd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5.name: Scotch Game: Tartakower Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 exd4 4.Nxd4 Nf6 5.strategy: Defends e4 with the knight and keeps the pawn structure intact, preferring a quieter game to the sharp lines. The cost is that the bishop on c1 stays shut in behind its own knight.

Defends e4 with a developing move and keeps the pawn structure intact, so Black's doubled c-pawns stay a long-term weakness. The price is a bishop that blocks the queen's file and no pressure on the centre: Black develops easily and strikes in the middle at once.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 exd4 4.Nxd4 Nxd4.name: Scotch Game: Lolli Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 exd4 4.Nxd4 Nxd4.background: The Lolli Variation, 3...Nxd4, was popular in the nineteenth century and received five columns of analysis in Freeborough and Ranken's 1896 manual Chess Openings Ancient and Modern.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 exd4 4.Nxd4 Nxd4.strategy: Recaptures with the queen, which lands on the central d4 square where nothing can easily chase it, since Black has traded away the knight that would have hit it. White gets an active queen and the more comfortable game.
Hits the knight with a pawn instead of recapturing it, but the knight just steps back and White is left a knight down with nothing to show for it.
Develops with an eye on f7 but forgets to recapture: the knight simply steps back and White is a knight down without compensation.

Takes e5 and c5 away from the queen and frees the c8 bishop, but it does nothing about White's lead in development. The queen stays on d4, White develops with tempo, and Black is left defending a worse game.
Steps back so the knight can return to c6 and chase the queen, but it shuts in the f8 bishop and costs a tempo. White develops freely and keeps an edge.

Attacks the queen on d4 and offers a trade that would leave Black level. White has to deal with it before developing, so the queen cannot rule the centre; this is the most accurate way to meet the early exchange.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 exd4 4.Nxd4 Nxd4.name: Scotch Game: Ghulam-Kassim Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 exd4 4.Nxd4 Nxd4.strategy: Defends e4 and develops, but the bishop blocks the d-file behind the queen and creates no pressure. Black develops freely and equalises; White has given away the edge that Nc3 keeps.

Develops the knight to its natural square and guards e4, leaving the queen on d4 where it cannot easily be chased away. White leads in development and has the more active pieces, a small but lasting edge.
Puts the bishop on a natural diagonal, aimed at f7, but Black simply develops with ...Nf6 and ...Be6 and challenges it. White has little to show for it, and the clear edge that Nc3 keeps is gone.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 exd4 4.Nxd4 Qh4 5.name: Scotch Game: Steinitz Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 exd4 4.Nxd4 Qh4 5.strategy: Defends e4 and develops a piece, daring Black to win the pawn anyway. After the pin ...Bb4 White lets it go for a lead in development and play against the king; the extra pawn rarely makes up for Black's awkwardly placed king.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 exd4 4.Nxd4 Qh4 5.name: Scotch Game: Horwitz Attack
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 exd4 4.Nxd4 Qh4 5.strategy: Threatens Nxc7+ and leaves e4 to the queen. It is an established try, but after ...Bb4+ and ...Qxe4+ Black holds the pawn in a balanced game, while Nc3 keeps a clear edge: White spends its advantage for a sharper game.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 exd4 4.Nxd4 Qh4 5.name: Scotch Game: Braune Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 exd4 4.Nxd4 Qh4 5.strategy: Develops the bishop and backs up the d4 knight, but does not guard e4, so Black takes the pawn. White gets a lead in development for it, but that only balances the game, while the main line keeps a clear edge.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 exd4 4.Nxd4 Qh4 5.name: Scotch Game: Fraser Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 exd4 4.Nxd4 Qh4 5.strategy: Retreats with tempo on the queen so that White can castle quickly, but the e4 pawn goes with check. White gets a lead in development in return, but that only balances the game, where defending with Nc3 keeps a clear edge.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 exd4 4.Nxd4 Qh4 5.name: Scotch Game: Paulsen Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 exd4 4.Nxd4 Qh4 5.strategy: Attacks the queen, but the knight lands where ...Qxe4+ takes a pawn with check and hits it. White can keep the knight only by retreating it to e3, where it is pinned to the king; any other block loses the knight on f5.
Checks first, so White must answer before Nxc7+ can be played, and the capture on e4 follows safely. Black keeps the extra pawn in a balanced game, though the king may stay in the centre.

Takes the pawn at once, but this move order lets White play Be2 with Nc3 to follow, and the king still has to go to d8 to save c7. White ends up better: an awkward king costs more than the extra pawn.
Threatens mate on f2 with queen and bishop, so White has to defend at once. But c7 stays loose to the knight, and the queen move that guards f2 also develops, so White keeps the initiative.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 exd4 4.Nxd4 Qh4 5.name: Scotch Game
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 exd4 4.Nxd4 Qh4 5.strategy: Blocks the check with a developing move that also attacks the bishop, so Black must decide at once whether to trade or take on e4. The knight on b5 still eyes c7, which keeps pressure on Black's king.

Blocks the check with a pawn that also attacks the bishop, so Black has to react at once while the knight on b5 still threatens c7. The pawn gives the knights a solid base but takes the natural square from the b1 knight.

Blocks with the b1 knight, which also guards e4, so no pawn is lost. But the knight is pinned and Black can take it: recapturing with the b-pawn gives up e4, and recapturing with the other knight pulls it away from c7, so the attack fades.
Wins the pawn with check, but White's knight still threatens c7, which is why the king typically goes to d8 and loses the right to castle. Black's extra pawn comes at the price of a harassed king.
Trades the bishop at once, but the b1 knight recaptures and guards e4, so the pawn grab is gone while the knight on b5 still threatens c7. Black spends time on defence and is worse for it.
Develops and attacks e4 a second time, and keeps castling available. White can win the pawn on c7 after Qe2 and ...O-O, but Black regains e4 with active pieces, and the game is balanced.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 exd4 4.Nxd4 Qh4 5.name: Scotch Game: Modern Defence
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 exd4 4.Nxd4 Qh4 5.strategy: Pins the knight that defends e4, so Black wins the pawn. The price is time: White gets a lead in development, and Black's awkwardly placed king tends to matter more than the extra pawn. The most testing answer to White's main line.
Attacks e4 a second time, but White ignores the pawn: g3 drives the queen back, and after the queen trade Ndb5 attacks c7. Black loses material for nothing, and White ends up winning.
Trades the knight and lets the queen recapture on d4, where it eyes g7 while the c3 knight keeps e4 safe. Black loses time and the pressure on e4 disappears, so White's lead in development stays.
